design: Non-LLM bibliometric predictors of the ensemble's inclusion decision, computed from library-stored metadata and record text only. Convergent validity: an independent signal that agrees on topic but not on prestige is evidence the screener judges relevance.
provenance: Every figure in this file comes from one code path -- validation/llm_screen_validate.py bibliometric -- run once per corpus on the full scored pool. Earlier versions of this file mixed those values with figures from an ad-hoc notebook computation, which disagreed in the third decimal and, for the top-rank comparison, in the count. Regenerate with that command rather than editing numbers here.
basis: full scored pool (all records the ensemble scored), per corpus

range_restriction.note: Restricting to gate survivors removes the easy exclusions, so the topical predictor's apparent discrimination falls -- most sharply in the large corpus (0.664 to 0.545). The full-pool figure supports the claim 'the screener tracks topic'; the survivor figure supports the weaker claim 'it discriminates among borderline records'. Both are reported with their basis named, because quoting only the higher one would overstate the evidence.

top_rank_note: Overlap between the 250 records the ensemble ranked highest and the 250 ranked highest by tf-idf similarity to the seed centroid. Substantial in the favourable corpus (89/250 = 36% against a chance rate of 10%) and moderate in the large one (40/250 = 16% vs 8%), but only 23/250 = 9.2% against a chance rate of 6.3% in the adverse corpus -- barely above chance there, so this comparison supports the convergence claim in two corpora and not the third. Partial overlap is expected and desirable: identical rankings would mean the model added nothing over tf-idf.

seed_convergence.note: The adverse seed set contains a structural-biology paper admitted by the Boolean query. Leave-one-out TF-IDF similarity to the other 14 seeds ranks it last, and the LLM ensemble scores it 1.0 -- the lowest of the fifteen. Two methods sharing no machinery agree that the seed, not the screener, was the problem.

keyword_overlap.note: Scopus author and index keywords are human-assigned metadata and would be the most attractive predictor, but only 1.9% of screened records appear in the export at all (47 of 2,515 in the favourable case), leaving 32 with both a keyword list and a decision. Too few for an estimate; reported as not usable rather than as a null result.

interpretation: The pattern is the finding. Topical similarity to the seed set tracks the ensemble's decisions in every corpus (0.6736, 0.7702, 0.664) while prestige predictors do not: citation count averages 0.474, at or below chance, and reference-list length 0.540. A screener that rewarded well-cited or well-connected work would show the opposite pattern, and that is the specific failure mode a positive control cannot detect, because the papers a reviewer chooses as seeds are themselves well-cited. Publication year is the exception worth naming: 0.6842 in the adverse corpus, which spans 1971-2025, so recency carries genuine topical information there. Field coverage is near-complete for every predictor (see auc_class_counts), so none of these figures rests on a reduced subset; what does vary by basis is range restriction, reported under range_restriction.
auc_class_counts_note: n_ensemble_included / n_ensemble_excluded are the AUC's POSITIVE and NEGATIVE classes -- records the LLM ensemble included versus excluded at tau -- not present versus missing data. Field missingness is reported separately as n_missing_field: a record is dropped from a predictor's AUC only when that predictor's value is absent. For cited_by the missing counts are adverse 159/3998, mid 2/2500, large 1/3000. A citation count of 0 is a real measured value, not a gap: 42 of the 311 records in validation/validation_records.json have cited_by_count == 0, and OpenAlex independently reports 0 for each of the six checked, so they are uncited papers rather than unknowns.
